## Economy and resources

**Economy and resources (direction decided 21 October 2026; the first phase is build order item 9+, and the later phases are specced before they get a place).** Today gold is the only thing kings can exchange, and it buys only what anyone can buy, so the only reasons left for kings to deal kindly with each other are fear and balance. The letters are mostly about goods. Alashiya's king writes to Pharaoh as a brother though his is a small power, because he has copper (EA 35), and every court has something another lacks. Goods make dealing positive-sum and give blockades, piracy, interception and route choice something worth stopping. Same rules, different data: a province produces goods, goods travel as cargo with characters on the same roads and errands as everything else, and some things need inputs.

**Six resources.** A resource earns its place only if it is unevenly spread, so courts depend on each other; worth carrying far, so trade happens; and feeds something nothing else feeds.

- **Grain** feeds people and armies, and grows everywhere ("Grain is everywhere, the surplus is not" below).
- **Copper:** Alashiya above all, with smaller sources such as the Ergani mines by Isuwa, which Hatti and Mitanni fought over ("Alashiya, the copper island" below).
- **Tin** comes from beyond the map, overland from the east and by sea from the west ("Edge markets" below). Copper and tin together make bronze, and no court has both; copper alone arms men less well ("Three levels of arms" below).
- **Timber:** the cedar of Lebanon, for ships and chariots. Egypt had none of its own.
- **Horses,** for chariots, from the grasslands: Mitanni's steppe in Upper Mesopotamia (the Kikkuli horse-training manual, written for the Hittites, is the work of a trainer from Mitanni), Hatti's Anatolian plateau, Babylonia through the Kassites, who came from the Zagros and were known for their horses, and Assyria, whose king Ashur-uballit sent Pharaoh a chariot and two horses with his first letter (EA 15). Egypt bred few and relied on tribute and gifts from Asia, so the gold power needs its rivals' horses for its chariots.
- **Gold:** precious metal, called gold in the game, with Egypt and Nubia by far the largest source ("Precious metal, called gold" below).

Left out: **stone**, never traded in bulk, since people built with what was at hand (Babylonia in mud brick), so it is part of the gold cost of building, perhaps dearer by terrain; and **cattle**, counted in each province's food and carrying capacity. Herds do one thing grain does not: they walk with their people and can be driven off (the Kaska raided Hittite lands for cattle, and the Suteans lived from their flocks), so they may come back to give the herding lands a life of their own. Pack donkeys are part of what a caravan costs.

**Everyday goods are part of the gold cost (decided 21 October 2026).** What every province makes for itself, such as stone, donkeys, oxen, cloth, oil, fuel and tools, is not a resource: it is bought where it is needed and folded into the gold cost of whatever uses it, a caravan's donkeys into the caravan, a wall's stone into the wall. Gold pays for it as it pays for labour ("Gold buys labour"), because no court could squeeze another over something every market sells. That is a price, not magic: the goods are there, and only their trade is too ordinary to be worth a rule. Donkeys show the line well. Old Assyrian merchants bought them at Assur and sold them in Anatolia at the end of the road along with the cargo, so donkeys were traded, but as a cheap, local, everyday purchase. Horses fail none of the three tests: they were bred only in certain grasslands, they were essential for chariots, and kings sent them to each other as royal gifts. So horses are a resource and donkeys are not, though both are animals that carry things. When a good starts to matter between courts, by those three tests, it can become a resource; until then it stays in the price.

**Precious metal, called gold (decided 21 October 2026).** In the code the resource is precious metal; on screen it has the gold icon; kings and characters call it gold, as the letters do, and the rulebook says once that "gold" covers all precious metal, Hatti's silver included. Its worth shows in yield rather than in a second metal: a gold mine yields more than a silver mine of the same size. Egypt and Nubia were by far the largest source, which is why the other kings kept writing to Pharaoh for gold, but not the only one: Hatti had the silver of the Taurus. The river gold of western Anatolia, the Pactolus that later gave Lydia its electrum, stays off the map: its fame is some seven centuries later, and nothing shows it was worked in 1346 ("Places in their own time"; decided 27 October 2026, answering item 6+'s review). Precious metal comes only from mines on the map: metal did not appear in harbours from nowhere, it arrived because something else left in exchange, which is what the edge markets are for (below). So Egypt is the largest supplier but cannot starve anyone, and the others have a reason to compete on price.

**Mines are where they were (decided 21 October 2026).** Every source of a resource sits where it was in the period and yields as much as it did, as far as the sources tell; the history pass (build order item 6+) finds them. Absolute outputs are mostly unknown, so what matters is the proportions, from whatever evidence there is, such as the Uluburun wreck of about 1300 BCE, which carried some ten tons of copper and one of tin, the proportions of bronze. Where the sources are silent, the dossier says so and the figure is a marked estimate.

**Alashiya, the copper island.** As the largest source of copper, Alashiya holds a position far beyond its armies: a lottery winner in a lawless world. Its own forests fuelled its smelting, so its timber cannot be cut off. What it depends on is tin, without which its copper makes no bronze even for itself; gold to pay its men; and grain in a bad year. If it tries to starve others of copper, they can cut off its tin. Its greater danger is invasion, and its protection is that everyone else needs the copper to keep flowing, so whoever seizes the island faces all the rest.

**Edge markets (decided 21 October 2026).** The world beyond the map is a set of markets at its borders: off-map trading partners that sell what the map lacks and buy what they want, for a price, by the same market rules as any city, with their supply and demand set as data instead of grown on the map. The map is not stretched to reach them. The tin mines lay thousands of kilometres away, across land with no courts of the Amarna system, no letters and little evidence, and the kings themselves did not know where tin came from: they saw it arrive from the east, or by sea. The map ends where their world ended. An edge market is also truer than metal appearing in a harbour, since tin arrives only if something goes the other way: chiefly gold, which leaves the map with it, so the edges are also a natural outlet for the gold the mines keep adding.

Tin comes from two edges:

- **East, overland.** From Central Asia, through Iran into Elam, then along the road held by Babylonia and Assyria and up the Euphrates to Syria, the coast and Alashiya. Elam, a free state on the map, becomes the tin gate, and the Middle Euphrates towns pass the tin west.
- **West, by sea.** From beyond the western sea zones, arriving on Arzawa's coast, at Alashiya and in the Levantine ports.

The split between them is a live debate. Wayne Powell's study (2022) traced about a third of the Uluburun wreck's tin to Central Asia and about two thirds to Kestel in the Taurus, in Hatti's lands, a working others dispute and that is unproven for the period; so tin stays off the map, split evenly between the two edges, and no mine on the map gives a court its own tin (decided 27 October 2026, answering item 6+'s review). A 2025 study in *Antiquity* by Alan Williams and colleagues matched tin ingots from two wrecks off Israel, about 3,300 years old, to Cornwall and Devon, and argues that British tin reached the eastern Mediterranean by about 1400 BCE and outweighed Central Asian tin in the late Bronze Age; Powell disagrees ([Science News](https://www.sciencenews.org/article/british-tin-bronze-age-civilizations)). The history pass weighs the debate and sets the split, marked in its dossier as disputed. Two roads also make better play than one: if Babylonia closes the eastern road, the sea powers still bring tin from the west, and the other way round, so no single power can choke bronze. One smaller edge completes the ring: Magan at the end of the Gulf, selling a little copper ("What each edge trades", below).

**What each edge trades (decided 27 October 2026).** Each edge market sells what the world of the letters drew from beyond it and buys what that world sent back, in amounts the history pass sets as first guesses. Every market buys gold, so the edges are the main way gold leaves the map ("Where gold comes from and where it goes"), and none sells precious metal, since the mines on the map are the only new gold.

- **The eastern road, beyond Susa:** sells the eastern share of tin; buys gold.
- **Keftiu and Ahhiyawa, beyond the western sea:** sells the western share of tin; buys gold and copper, as the Aegean took Egypt's gold and Cyprus's copper.
- **Magan, at the end of the Gulf:** sells a little copper; buys gold and grain, as it took Mesopotamia's silver and barley.
- **Punt, at the end of the Red Sea, has no market.** Its trade was in incense, ebony and gold: the first two are not resources, and its gold would be new gold, so a market there would add nothing the game counts. If the Red Sea is added ("The Red Sea" under Ideas), Punt is a door for newcomers only.

Pottery, oil, cloth and the other goods that also travelled stay out of trade until one meets the tests for a resource ("Six resources").

**Who has what.** Every great power has something to sell and something it must buy. A first sketch, with the history pass setting the real sources and proportions:

- **Egypt:** gold and grain; it buys horses, timber, copper and tin.
- **Babylonia:** grain and horses, and the tin road from the east.
- **Assyria:** horses, and the tin road.
- **Mitanni:** horses, and the Euphrates crossing that eastern tin takes going west.
- **Hatti:** horses and silver, with Isuwa's copper within reach, and grain that fails in drought.
- **Arzawa:** the timber of its western forests, and the coast where western tin and the Aegean's trade land.
- **Alashiya:** copper, and its own timber.
- **The Lebanese coast** (Byblos and its neighbours): timber.
- **Elam:** the gate to eastern tin.

**Production is local (decided 21 October 2026).** Every resource is produced by a province, and how much it yields depends on:

- its population, since people are the labour;
- how well fed they are: hungry people produce less, and move away;
- its land, climate and the season ("Land and climate", "Seasons", "Rivers"), with effects that differ by resource: a harvest comes in its season and follows the flood or the rains;
- what has been built there and kept up, such as canals, granaries, roads and policing ("Gold buys labour");
- war: armies fighting, foraging or looting there, and men levied from it, since every man under arms is a man not in the fields or the mines;
- catastrophes.

What a province produces stays where it was made, in its stores, until someone moves it. So a kingdom must carry its own goods, grain from the Delta to Gaza's depot or copper from the mines to the coast (gold alone follows its own rule: "One treasury, many stores"), by the same carriers, roads and dangers as any trade, and its roads and rivers matter at home as much as abroad. A province's stores fall with it. Losing a province loses its production, and winning one does not bring its full output at once: the war has damaged it, its people may have fled, and it yields more only as it recovers and is absorbed.

**Feeding a province draws its people (decided 21 October 2026).** Settled people move between neighbouring provinces of a kingdom towards more room ("Where people go" under "People of the land"), and room is measured in food: what the land can carry plus the grain in the province's stores. So a province stocked well above its needs pulls people harder, in proportion to how far its food exceeds its people's needs compared with its neighbour's. Since people are a province's labour, a king who keeps grain flowing to a mine province fills it faster and raises its output. The pull lasts only as long as the grain does: when the supply stops, the extra people go hungry and move on, or flee across the border. Egypt fed its expeditions to the mines and quarries from the state's stores, and a generation later Seti I had a well dug on the desert road to the gold mines because the miners could not live there without water.

**Storage (decided 21 October 2026).** How much a province can hold is set by a basic capacity from its towns, raised by what is built there: granaries and silos for grain, which also slow its spoiling, and storehouses for other goods. Without them a surplus is lost, so storage is an investment in the provinces that matter: a mine province fed from its stores, a depot on an army's road, a granary against drought. Full stores are also a prize, since a province's stores fall with it.

**Caravans carry a kingdom's goods (decided 21 October 2026, as a start).** A kingdom's routine shipments, such as grain to a depot or an army, or copper to the coast, travel as caravans: porters and guards levied from the settled people like soldiers, men in a unit rather than characters, so a caravan on the road is also hands missing from the fields. Like soldiers, they are paid in gold and fed with grain they carry as part of the load, which is why grain carried overland eats much of its own value; unpaid, they desert, and hungry, they eat the cargo first and then desert. The realm's couriers follow the same rules, a few men each. A caravan's size is its sender's choice: a large one carries more but moves more slowly and is easier to find, and a small company is quick and discreet. So a big army is supplied by depots stocked ahead on its road and small companies shuttling after it, given gold to buy food along the way wherever they have passage ("Armies need food as well as pay"). A caravan follows its scheduled orders, can be robbed or intercepted, and decides nothing. A character leading it adds judgement: a safer route, a bargain over a toll, or the chance that he steals it all. Caravans may cross borders too, since handing over goods needs no language: one can deliver a sale or a tribute already agreed, and it can sell and buy at a foreign market it has passage to, since the engine sets the prices and there is nothing to bargain over (decided 21 October 2026), so kingdoms trade from the first phase and price gaps between markets pay. Agreeing anything else needs someone who speaks, and letters and tablets always travel with a character, because a tablet must be accompanied by talk ("No faceless channel"). This is where it starts, to be revisited once games show what happens on the roads.

**Ships carry goods (decided 21 October 2026).** A ship is a company at sea: the rules for caravans and for a company's pace hold ("What sets a company's pace"), with a capacity far beyond any land caravan. The Uluburun ship of about 1300 BCE carried some ten tons of copper and a ton of tin, with glass, ebony, ivory and gold besides, and a crew of perhaps a dozen, while a donkey carried some 65 kg: one ship did the work of hundreds of donkeys. It moves by current, wind and the sailing season along coastal waters and open-sea crossings ("Finer seas"), and on the rivers by their own rules ("Rivers").

- **Building.** A ship is built in a harbour from timber, with gold for the shipwrights, and crewed by levied sailors, paid and fed like porters. So the cedar of Lebanon is strategic, Egypt depends on Byblos for its ships, and harbours earn their place ("One rule for everything built").
- **Passage on others' ships.** A character may be a ship's captain who carries other people's goods for a fee, as Ugarit's merchants did. He sells passage as a carrier sells a carry job, with the same divided loyalty.
- **Cargo or war.** The same ship carries cargo or fights, and its king chooses which; merchant ships were pressed into war fleets, so the line was thin then too. A loaded ship fights badly, and a warship carries little.
- **What keeps the land alive.** The sea grows dangerous in winter ("Winter is dangerous, never closed"), storms and pirates take ships in the same check as nature and outlaws on land, a blockade decides at sea, a ship needs a harbour at both ends, and a sea ship cannot go inland, though river boats work the Nile and the Euphrates by their own rules. So bulk goods and long distances go by sea in the sailing season, and inland routes, winter journeys and anything that must not be caught at sea go by land.
- **What waters are worth.** A sea zone earns nothing by itself; it is a road. Its worth is what flows along it and who can tax, protect or stop it: the edge market at its far end and the price gaps between its ports, the tolls its harbours charge, the cheaper transport that lets a coast sell its grain dearer and buy its copper cheaper, and the power of a fleet that holds its coastal waters to blockade, to protect its own trade or to raid another's.
- **Ships carried overland (decided 21 October 2026).** A ship can be taken apart into a load, a very heavy one that oxcarts carry slowly under the pace rule ("What sets a company's pace"), and put together again at a shore, for time and the shipwrights' gold. It was done in this very period: Thutmose III had boats built of cedar near Byblos and carried on ox-carts to the Euphrates, so that his army crossed into Mitanni where nobody expected it, and Egypt's Red Sea fleets were built in pieces, partly of Lebanese cedar, carried across the Eastern Desert from the Nile and assembled on the coast, where ship timbers have been found at Mersa Gawasis. It needs no new machinery, since a ship in pieces is cargo like any other, and it allows surprise: an army crossing a river where nobody has boats, or a fleet appearing on waters it could not sail to. Built with shipbuilding from timber, in the economy's later phases.

Ships carry cargo from the economy's first phase (item 9+b) with the fleets the game already has, and every coastal province starts with a harbour level, as policing starts with a base level, until item 15 makes harbours a built level; timber as the input to shipbuilding comes with the later phases.

**Grain is everywhere, the surplus is not.** Every province grows food by its land and climate ("Land and climate"), so every court feeds itself in a normal year. What varies is the surplus and how reliable it is:

- Irrigated land (Egypt, Babylonia) gives large surpluses but swings with its river: a low Nile is a bad year for all Egypt.
- Rain-fed land (Hatti, most of Syria) feeds itself but is hit hard by drought, which is why Hatti in the end needed Egyptian grain.
- Alashiya feeds itself from its central plain; its trade is copper.
- Coastal cities with small hinterlands live on imports: Abi-milku of Tyre, on his island, kept asking Pharaoh for water and wood, and Rib-Hadda of Byblos begged for grain whenever his fields were cut off.

Everyone stands to gain from more, since food sets how many people a province holds, and people are labour, soldiers and taxes. So grain is wanted by cities with too little land, armies in the field, lands in drought, and kings who want to grow. It is heavy: by ship or river it is cheap to move, overland it eats much of its own value, so the coast, the Nile and the Euphrates carry it, and blockades have something to strangle.

**Gold buys labour.** Goods are what things are made of; gold is what makes people do the work. Whatever needs materials costs goods and whatever needs people costs gold, so gold is an input to almost everything and has value for what it does, not because a rule names it money.

- **Armies.** Soldiers are paid in gold and fed with grain, two needs that fail in different ways ("Armies need food as well as pay" below). Unpaid soldiers desert or become bands, as decided.
- **Arms.** Raising or arming a unit uses up metal from the king's stores, copper alone or copper and tin for bronze ("Three levels of arms" below), plus gold for the smiths and the men. There are no workshops.
- **Ships.** Timber, plus gold for shipwrights and crew. Porters and sailors are paid in gold too.
- **Building.** Walls (the existing walls and sieges); roads (travel times and route choice, which answers who pays in item 15: whoever invests); policing, meaning fewer robberies and interceptions by bands on the province's roads and likely less unrest (Egypt's Medjay are a model); and food production, canals and granaries that raise carrying capacity, with granaries softening drought. What is built decays without upkeep, as Mesopotamia's canals silted, so the land does not pile up improvements forever, a well-kept province is worth taking, and armies have something to destroy. The random ending makes long investments look worse as the omens darken, so kings stop building and spend on armies and bribes as the age ends, with no rule for it.

**One rule for everything built (decided 21 October 2026).** Every kind of building is a level in a province, with the same three parts:

- **Upkeep:** each level costs gold every season; paid, it holds.
- **Decay:** unpaid, it falls, at a rate set by its kind.
- **Building:** gold beyond upkeep starts a project that raises the level over the seasons that follow, at a pace set by its kind, so a canal is not dug in one season. A project shows how far it has come and when it will be done ("canal: two-thirds dug, done in two seasons"), so a king can judge it by its return over a horizon he can name ("Gold is a lifeline"). Its gains arrive gradually after he pays, which feels like momentum in play without the lags and overshoots of a model of momentum.

The kinds differ only in data:

| Kind | What it does | Decay without upkeep |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Walls | defence and sieges | very slow, over decades |
| Roads and relay stations | faster travel, messages and orders | slow, over years |
| Fields: canals and terraces | more food and capacity, softer droughts | fast, since canals silt |
| Mines | output where the ore is | medium, as shafts flood and workers drift away |
| Storage: granaries and storehouses | capacity, slower spoilage | slow |
| Harbours | ships based and trading there, a besieged coast supplied | slow |
| Policing | fewer bandits, smugglers caught | almost at once |

Policing shows why one rule is enough: it is not built at all but paid people, so it is gone within a season of stopping, where a wall stands for decades; the same rule with a different rate. The land sets limits: canals only where there is water to lead, mines only where the ore is, walls around towns, harbours on a coast. War interrupts projects, since the workers flee; an occupying army can raze what stands, and a siege damages walls. A conqueror takes over what stands, and its upkeep with it. Item 15 builds the rule for roads, relay stations, policing and harbours and brings item 5's walls into it; the economy's later phases add fields, mines and storage through it.
